title: The role of the big geographic sort in online news circulation among U.S. Reddit users
screen_reason: Although the paper's aim is to explain state-level variation in news circulation, its Data and Results sections report the descriptive composition of news-link sharing on Reddit with explicit denominators: Table 1 gives 116,212 comments carrying fake-news links and 536,701 carrying low-credibility links out of the 8.2M comments containing news links (text: 'a total of 8.23M (0.6%) comments containing news links'), and the text states that 1.7% of geotagged users posted at least one comment containing a fake news URL. These are observed sharing shares from platform data, so SHARING rows (content_share and actor_share) are extractable, plus one source-concentration statement.

estimates.measure_type: % of Reddit comments containing news links whose link pointed to a fake-news domain
estimates.value_raw: Table 1: Fake = 116,212 unique comments; Lowcred = 536,701; Reputable = 7,645,044 (sum 8,297,957 news-link comments; the text states the total as 'a total of 8.23M (0.6%) comments containing news links'). 116,212/8,297,957 = 1.4% (1.41% on the text's 8.23M).
estimates.denominator: All Reddit comments containing a news URL posted by the ~3M users geolocated to one of the 50 U.S. states, January 2016 - December 2019 (8.2M comments; text: 8.23M)
estimates.definition: A comment counted in the numerator if the news URL it contained pointed to one of 933 domains classified 'fake', i.e. domains that, per five source lists, had 'routinely published completely fabricated news articles'.
estimates.misinfo_def: "we categorized a domain as fake if it had routinely published completely fabricated news articles"; low-credibility domains "publish articles with mixed factualness rather than completely fabricated content" and were "described by the previous 5 sources as unreliable, hyperpartisan, clickbait, rumor, pseudoscience, and conspiracy sites"
estimates.source_quote: table content: 7.6M (93%) comments contained reputable news articles, while only 116.2K contained fake news articles.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Classification of news comments' (p. 3), and Table 1 (p. 3) for the exact counts
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Publisher-level (domain) labelling into fake / lowcred / reputable. Fake and lowcred lists compiled from five sources: the Zimdars list, Media Bias/Fact Check, PolitiFact, the Daily Dot, and Allcott et al. (933 fake domains, 1,801 low-credibility domains); reputable from Vargo et al., Alexa and Media Bias/Fact Check (8.9k sites, 5,221 of them observed). Validated against professional fact-checkers' trustworthiness scores: mean 0.66 reputable, 0.10 low-credibility, 0.02 fake. The authors note publisher-level attribution is less precise than article-level.
estimates.moderator_quote: From these 1.4B comments, we identified a total of 8.23M (0.6%) comments containing news links (as URLs). We then classified a Reddit comment as either reputable, fake, or low credibility based on the domain that the news URL pointed to
estimates.notes: The percentage is not printed; it is the exact part/whole share of two verbatim counts with the same denominator (numerator 116,212 from Table 1; whole = all news-link comments, stated in text as 8.23M and summing to 8,297,957 across Table 1's three rows). It rounds to 1.4% on either denominator, so the small text/table discrepancy does not matter at one decimal. year = 2018 as the (nearest whole-year) midpoint of the four-year collection window, per the collapse-a-time-series rule; the full span is in date. breadth left blank because falsity is assigned by domain list, not per item (the fake vs low-credibility contrast is carried by definition/definition_variant instead). Denominator is news-carrying comments, not all Reddit comments: the share of ALL geolocated comments that carried a fake-news link would be 116,212/1.4B ~ 0.008%, which the paper does not state. QUOTE FIX (validator pass): source_quote now holds the single contiguous sentence carrying the numerator (116.2K fake-news comments, the rounded form of Table 1's 116,212); the earlier version spliced that sentence to a Table 1 row with '||' and was not a contiguous span. The denominator sentence stays in moderator_quote and the exact table counts in value_raw.

estimates.measure_type: % of Reddit comments containing news links whose link pointed to a low-credibility domain (broader definition)
estimates.value_raw: Table 1: Lowcred = 536,701 unique comments of 8,297,957 news-link comments (Table 1 sum; text total 8.23M) = 6.5%
estimates.denominator: All Reddit comments containing a news URL posted by the ~3M users geolocated to one of the 50 U.S. states, January 2016 - December 2019 (8.2M comments; text: 8.23M)
estimates.definition: A comment counted in the numerator if the news URL it contained pointed to one of 1,801 'low-credibility' domains - sites described by the five source lists as unreliable, hyperpartisan, clickbait, rumor, pseudoscience or conspiracy, publishing content of mixed factualness rather than wholly fabricated.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Unlike fake news sites, low-credibility news sites publish articles with mixed factualness rather than completely fabricated content. We included domains that were described by the previous 5 sources as unreliable, hyperpartisan, clickbait, rumor, pseudoscience, and conspiracy sites, ending up with a total of 1801 low-credibility news domains."
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same five-source domain lists as the fake-news row; low-credibility is the looser tier (1,801 domains). Validation against fact-checker trust scores gave a mean of 0.10 for low-credibility sites vs 0.66 reputable and 0.02 fake.
estimates.moderator_quote: Using the compiled domain credibility lists, we labelled individual news articles with corresponding domain labels. Hence, we attributed misinformation at the level of the publisher (i.e., domain) and not at the level of the individual news article
estimates.notes: Marked definition_variant because this is the looser 'low-credibility' tier of the same measure as the fake-news row in the same country x platform cell. The two must NOT be added: 1.4 + 6.5 = 7.9 would be a cross-category sum, which the value keep rule forbids (the paper never prints a combined non-reputable share; its own '93% reputable' is likewise a rounded figure whose complement I did not take). QUOTE FIX (validator pass): source_quote is now the verbatim Table 1 row as rendered in the text file (News_type, Unique_comments, Unique_user, Unique_news_site, Unique_urls = Lowcred 536701 160146 1801 264010); the earlier version prefixed 'Table 1:' and appended the top-sites cell, so it was not verbatim.

estimates.measure_type: % of US-geolocated Reddit users who posted at least one comment containing a fake-news URL
estimates.value_raw: 1.7% of all geotagged users had posted at least 1 comment containing fake news URLs
estimates.denominator: Approximately 3M Reddit users geolocated to one of the 50 U.S. states (users who had posted in at least one of 2.87K state-matched subreddits), January 2016 - December 2019
estimates.definition: A user counted in the numerator if at least one of their comments over the four years contained a URL to one of the 933 fake-news domains.
estimates.misinfo_def: "we categorized a domain as fake if it had routinely published completely fabricated news articles"
estimates.source_quote: We observed that the average numbers of comments posted by users of the two groups were comparable, with just a small difference: 1.7% of all geotagged users had posted at least 1 comment containing fake news URLs, whereas only 0.6% of non-geotagged users did.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same publisher-level lists (933 fake domains from Zimdars, MBFC, PolitiFact, Daily Dot, Allcott et al.), validated against fact-checker trust scores.
estimates.moderator_quote: We identified approximately 3M users who were located in one of the 50 U.S. states.
estimates.notes: This is an actor-share among platform users, not a survey, so denom_scope is population (the users at risk of sharing) and unit is account. Two caveats for the adjudicator: (a) the denominator is stated only as 'approximately 3M', and (b) Table 1's 45,485 unique fake-news-posting users over 3M would be 1.5%, slightly below the printed 1.7% (the printed figure may be computed on a slightly different user base); I kept the verbatim 1.7% and did not compute my own. Reddit users are geolocated by their posting in state subreddits, so 'US users' is inferred behaviourally, not self-reported.

estimates.measure_type: share of all fake-news comments accounted for by the single most-shared fake-news domain (breitbart.com)
estimates.value_raw: approximately one-fifth of all fake news comments contained URLs from breitbart.com (1 of 933 fake-news domains)
estimates.conc_group_label: The single top fake-news domain, breitbart.com (1 of the 933 fake-news domains in the list)
estimates.denominator: 116,212 Reddit comments containing links to fake-news domains
estimates.definition: Share of fake-news-link comments whose URL came from breitbart.com, the most-linked fake-news domain.
estimates.misinfo_def: "we categorized a domain as fake if it had routinely published completely fabricated news articles"
estimates.source_quote: Those low average values are due to the frequency distribution of the number of comments per news site being skewed: most news sites attract a few comments only, while a few attract most comments (e.g., approximately one-fifth of all fake news comments contained URLs from breitbart.com).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same publisher-level fake/lowcred/reputable lists; breitbart.com is listed in Table 1 as the top fake-news site by comment volume.
estimates.moderator_quote: most news sites attract a few comments only, while a few attract most comments (e.g., approximately one-fifth of all fake news comments contained URLs from breitbart.com)
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL - drop this row if the review requires exact stated values. Two weaknesses: the share is the paper's own approximation ('approximately one-fifth' = 20%, not a printed number), and conc_group_pct (0.1%) is my computation, 1 of the 933 fake-news domains, which the paper does not state as a percentage. I kept it because it is the only source-concentration statement in the paper and both halves required by the concentration rule are present. Note the direction of the measure: concentration of fake-news SHARING across sources, computed inside the fake-news-only subset (a top-source share, which is the normal form for concentration, so within_misinfo_content is left false).

missed_or_uncertain: (1) 0.6% of NON-geotagged Reddit users posted at least one fake-news comment - a verbatim behavioural actor share, but it is a validation comparison group whose country is unknown (the authors say they 'are less likely to all be from the U.S.'), so I did not give it a row; an adjudicator wanting a Global-scope companion row could add it. (2) Low-credibility actor share is not printed; 160,146 users (Table 1) over 'approximately 3M' would be ~5.3%, but the denominator is approximate and the paper does not state the percentage, so no row. (3) Diffusion statistics are not prevalence or concentration of exposure/sharing and were left out: '74.8% of all reputable news articles were only posted by a single user ... and 86.7% by at most 2 users'; news URLs posted in 5+ states were '209.7K for (6.3% of) reputable news comments, 11.0 K for (4.8% of) low-credibility ones, and 2.23K for (4.2% of) fake ones'. These are cascade-breadth shares (how far an item travelled), not the share of content/exposure that was misinformation. (4) 8.23M news-link comments are 0.6% of the 1.4B geolocated comments - a news-vs-non-news share, not a misinformation share. (5) Mean comments per site (reputable 36, lowcred 26, fake 8) are intensity means over sites, not per-capita exposure of people, so no per_capita_intensity row. (6) All state-level regressions (scaling exponent beta ~ 1, R2 ~ 0.95, personality/culture/socioeconomic/political models in Table 3) are explanatory statistics with no share. (7) Table 1's unique_urls counts (60,754 fake; 264,010 lowcred; 3,319,213 reputable) would give a URL-level content share of 1.7% fake / 7.3% lowcred, i.e. a second denominator for the same idea; I extracted the comment-level version because it is the one the text discusses, and flag the URL-level alternative here rather than duplicating rows.

rob.design: Full-census observational study of Pushshift's public Reddit comment dump, January 2016 - December 2019 (all public and quarantined subreddits). Users geolocated by the Balsamo et al. method using 2.87K state-matched subreddits (majority state assigned; 82.4% of users posted in a single state, 3.8% unassigned), giving ~3M US-located users and 1.4B comments (35% of all comments), of which 8.23M contained news URLs. Misinformation attributed at publisher level from five widely used domain lists (933 fake, 1,801 low-credibility, 8.9k reputable); no human item-level coding and therefore no inter-coder reliability; construct validation instead compares list labels with professional fact-checkers' trustworthiness scores (0.66 / 0.10 / 0.02). Limitations acknowledged by the authors: publisher-level rather than article-level labelling, list heterogeneity, and Reddit's non-representativeness of the US population.
rob.item6_quote: By using the descriptions and granular labels of each of the five sources, we categorized a domain as fake if it had routinely published completely fabricated news articles. There were a total of 933 unique fake news sites across all five sources.
rob.item10_quote: The circulation of news on Reddit (Table 1) amounts mainly to reputable content: 7.6M (93%) comments contained reputable news articles, while only 116.2K contained fake news articles.
